title: Nested Decisions
description: Putting an if inside an if, when to use && instead, and how to keep it readable.

content.text: First the usher checks your ticket. Only if you have one do they ask your age. An `if` inside another `if` is called **nesting**.

steps.note: Outer question: ticket? Yes. Go inside.
Inner question, only asked of ticket holders: is `15 >= 18`? No.

out: This film is for adults only.

content.title: Outer first, then inner
content.outro: Without a ticket, the age question is never reached at all. Each level gets one more step of indent, and each `{` needs its `}` at the same level.

content.question: Change `hasTicket` to `false`. What prints?
options: This film is for adults only.
content.explain: The outer test fails, so C++ jumps to the outer `else`. The inner `if` is skipped entirely.

items.title: Nested
items.text: Two levels to hold in your head.

content.title: Same rule, two shapes
content.caption: When both must be true and there is nothing to do in between, `&&` is easier to read.

content.value: Nesting earns its place when each failure needs a **different** message. `&&` can only say the whole thing failed, not which half.

steps.note: The inner `else` explains exactly what failed.
out: Old enough, but not tall enough.

content.title: Three messages from two questions

content.question: With `age = 10` and `height = 1.50`, what prints?
options: Old enough, but not tall enough.
content.explain: `10 >= 12` is false, so the outer `else` runs. The height is never checked.

content.real: Testing a chair before you sit
content.concept: Checking a value before you use it
content.text: Dividing a whole number by zero crashes the program. Check first, and only do the risky step when it is safe.

output: There has to be at least one person!
content.caption: Inside the `if`, `people` cannot be 0, so the division is safe. Set `people` to 3 and it prints `Each pays 300`.

content.value: A variable declared inside a block, like `each`, only exists until that block's `}`. You cannot print `each` after the `if`. Declare it before the `if` when you need it afterwards.
content.title: Block variables stay in the block

content.question: Why is the division inside the `if` block?
options: So it only runs when people is not 0
content.explain: The block runs only when `people > 0`, so the program never divides by zero.

items.title: Deep
items.text: The one line that matters is buried.

items.title: Flat

content.title: Flatten a deep nest
content.caption: Around three levels, readers lose track of which condition they are inside.
Another way to flatten: name the combined condition in a `bool` first. `if (canOrder)` reads like a sentence.

content.value: In Module 6 you will move a block of decisions into a function of its own, the real cure for deep nesting. Until then, `&&` and a well named `bool` keep almost anything readable.
The outer chain picks the ticket type. An inner `if` adds a weekend surcharge, but only for tickets that cost money.

steps.note: The chain is done. Print the result.

content.title: Outer chain, inner detail
content.outro: The infant branch has no inner `if`: a free ticket stays free at the weekend.

content.question: With `age = 3` and `weekend = true`, what is printed?
content.explain: `3 < 5` is true, so the infant branch sets `price` to 0. It has no inner `if`, so no surcharge is added.

practice.question: Ask for a mark. If it is 40 or more print Passed, and inside that block also print With distinction when it is 75 or more. A failing mark should print Failed.
Rewrite this nested pair as a single `if` using `&&`, keeping the same message.
Ask for two numbers and divide the first by the second, but check the second is not zero first. Print a clear message instead of crashing.

quiz.question: When does the inner `if` of a nested pair get tested?
options: Always, at the same time as the outer one
Only when the outer condition was true
Only when the outer condition was false
quiz.explain: The inner `if` is an instruction inside the outer block, so it is only reached if the outer condition let the program in.

quiz.question: Both conditions must be true, and there is nothing to do in between. What is better?
quiz.explain: `&&` gives one level of indentation and one condition to read. Nesting is for when the branches actually differ.

quiz.question: What can nesting do that a single `&&` condition cannot?
options: Give a different message depending on which half failed
quiz.explain: `&&` only reports that the whole condition failed. Nesting gives each failure its own `else`, and so its own explanation.

quiz.question: Why put `if (people > 0)` around a division?
options: Because C++ requires a check before every division
So the division never runs with a zero, which would crash the program
quiz.explain: Whole-number division by zero has no answer and usually crashes the program. Checking the value first lets you print a clear message instead.

quiz.question: Your code is nested four levels deep. What is the best first move?
options: Remove the braces to save space
Combine conditions with `&&`, or name one in a bool variable
Leave it: depth does not matter
quiz.explain: Both flatten the code without changing what it does. Later you will also be able to move a block into a function of its own.
